name: biogears-sbml-sepsis
title: Simulation core — one sepsis model, every engine: composed, ensembled, orchestrated, benchmarked

campaign_docs.name: BioGears sepsis core in Antimony: extraction report (Sauro)
campaign_docs.path: investigations/biogears-sbml-sepsis/sources/BioGears sepsis core in Antimony extraction report.pdf

lead:
The simulation core takes one specification — the BioGears sepsis core, a
lumped-parameter whole-body physiology model (cardiovascular circuit, baroreflex,
capillary fluid/albumin exchange, and the McDaniel 2019 Acute Inflammatory
Response) — and runs it under interchangeable engines behind one typed interface:
the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ engine (viva-biogears), the exact SBML/Antimony
extraction integrated by roadrunner/CVODE (viva-tellurium), and a learned PyTorch
surrogate (viva-torch). Because each engine is a box over the same observable
ports, the core can compose them into workflows, sweep them as ensembles, pass a
model artifact from one to another, and profile their compute — the capabilities
this investigation puts in front of the INFLECT team, each as something you can
open and run.

at_a_glance.role: Start here — the one model, the three engines, and the four capabilities this investigation demonstrates.
COMPOSITION — the same sepsis spec run under BioGears, Tellurium, and the surrogate by swapping one box; shared observables overlaid.
ENSEMBLES — a severity × engine batch run as one orchestrated sweep, gathered into a single grid.
ORCHESTRATION / WORKFLOWS — the four verbs compose registered modules into a pipeline and hand an Antimony/SBML file between engines, no new simulation code.
PERFORMANCE — one run from seconds to hours across engines; where the compute goes (the stiff ODE solve) and the ~40,000× surrogate tier.
FIDELITY — the honest backbone: the engines agree on the inflammation core to within ~0.1%, and diverge in the hemodynamic layer (mechanism and timing).

how_to_read:
How the simulation core works, in one idea: a simulation is a COMPOSITE — a small
graph of PROCESSES and STEPS that read and write a shared, TYPED state. Each box in
the graph declares typed input and output ports; the core wires the boxes together
by matching ports to shared state paths and advances them in time. Because the
interface is the ports — not the engine behind them — any engine that exposes the
same observable ports is a drop-in. That is the whole trick: the BioGears sepsis
core is ONE specification, and three different engines are each wrapped as a box
over the same ports —
  - BioGearsProcess   — the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine;
  - TelluriumUTCStep  — the exact SBML/Antimony extraction, integrated by roadrunner (CVODE);
  - NeuralProcess     — a learned PyTorch surrogate of the same core.
Swapping engines is swapping ONE box's address. The wiring, the emitters that record
results, and the analysis are all unchanged. "Same spec, many engines" is not a
slogan here — it is what the typed-port interface buys you (study 01).

How the orchestration works, in four verbs: the unified workflow API exposes exactly
this over HTTP, thinly — every call just builds and runs a composite.
  1. LIST modules       (GET /modules)              — the registered boxes you can use.
  2. RUN one module     (POST /modules/{name}/call) — run one box as a 1-node composite.
  3. CONNECT a workflow (POST /workflows)           — a composite spec: nodes (boxes) + wires.
  4. RUN the workflow   (POST /workflows/{id}/run)  — advance the composite, read the outputs.
Study 03 is the running example: it connects modules into a pipeline and hands the
Antimony/SBML extraction from one engine to another. Study 02 runs the engines as an
ensemble; study 04 profiles where each spends compute. Full reference:
docs/workflow-api.md and docs/api.md.

glossary.definition: A runnable simulation: a graph of processes/steps wired through a shared typed state. The core advances it in time.

A box in the composite. A PROCESS advances one time interval per update (e.g. BioGears, the surrogate); a STEP runs once to completion (e.g. a full Tellurium time course, a math derivation). Both expose typed input/output ports.
The named, typed inputs and outputs a box declares. Engines that expose the same ports are interchangeable — this is why one sepsis spec runs under three engines by swapping one box.
A registered process/step, addressable by name (e.g. TelluriumUTCStep, NeuralProcess). Dozens are registered (this workspace lists 76 at GET /modules).
A composite built through the API: a list of nodes (modules) plus wires connecting one node's output port to another's input port.

list a module, run one module, connect modules into a workflow, run the workflow — the entire workflow API surface (GET /modules, POST /modules/{name}/call, POST /workflows, POST /workflows/{id}/run).
Running many configurations (here severity × engine) as one orchestrated batch and gathering their endpoints into a single comparison.
A learned neural approximation (viva-torch NeuralProcess) of an engine's per-step dynamics. Replaces the ODE solve with one forward pass: ~4-5 orders of magnitude faster, approximate.

biological_story:
Sepsis in BioGears is a race between an inflammatory response and the
cardiovascular system that keeps blood pressure up. A bacterial load seeds the
tissue; the Acute Inflammatory Response (McDaniel 2019) amplifies, tissue integrity
falls, capillaries leak, and fluid moves from blood to interstitium. The heart and
vasculature compensate — heart rate and vascular tone rise — until, in severe
sepsis, that compensation fatigues and pressure falls toward septic shock.

This is the model the simulation core runs under every engine. The inflammation half
of the race the SBML extraction translates faithfully: run against the real engine,
tissue integrity and pathogen load track it to within ~0.1% in both mild and
severe infection. The cardiovascular half is where the engines part — BioGears
carries a whole driven body (nutrition schedule, temperature, respiration, renal
fluid handling, nitric-oxide and fever vasodilation, continuous baroreflex control),
so even a controlled infection shows pressures wandering over ~10 mmHg, while the
autonomous extraction holds those inputs at baseline and traces smooth. Same clinical
outcome, different hemodynamic path to shock — the measured fidelity limit in study 05,
which is why the capabilities here are shown on a model whose edges are stated, not hidden.
hypothesis:
This investigation is a capabilities DEMONSTRATION, not a single hypothesis test:
the thesis is that the simulation core already does all four of the above on a
real model, with each capability shown by an artifact that runs. The one place a
genuine hypothesis lives is the fidelity backbone (study 05): the SBML extraction
reproduces the inflammation core to within ~0.1% but diverges from the BioGears engine
in the hemodynamic layer — a real, measured result that keeps the demonstration
credible.

executive.what_is_this:
A guided tour of the simulation core's capabilities on one real model. The same
BioGears sepsis core is run under three interchangeable engines (BioGears C++,
exact SBML/Tellurium, PyTorch surrogate) and used to demonstrate four things, each
a runnable artifact: COMPOSITION (study 01 — the same spec under three engines by
one node swap), ENSEMBLES (study 02 — a severity × engine batch in one sweep),
ORCHESTRATION/WORKFLOWS (study 03 — the four-verb API composes modules into a
pipeline and hands an Antimony/SBML file between engines), and PERFORMANCE
(study 04 — where the compute goes, and a ~40,000× surrogate tier). A fidelity
backbone (study 05) keeps it honest: where the engines agree, and where they do not.
executive.verdict:
The simulation core does all four, shown not told. ONE sepsis spec runs under
three interchangeable engines by swapping a single box (01); a severity × engine
batch runs as one orchestrated sweep (02); the four-verb workflow API composes
registered modules into a pipeline and passes the Antimony/SBML extraction from
one engine to another with no new simulation code (03); and the same run spans
4+ orders of magnitude of compute — BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium ~2.81 h, the
surrogate ~0.2 s — with the exact engines' time spent almost entirely in the
stiff 91-state ODE solve the surrogate replaces with one forward pass (04). The
demonstration stays honest (05): the extraction reproduces the inflammation core
to within ~0.1% but reaches septic shock by a different hemodynamic mechanism and on
a flipped timeline, and the surrogate is a fast APPROXIMATE tier (bounded, not yet
clinically accurate), not a drop-in replacement.
executive.verdict_detail:
Each capability is a runnable artifact in its study: the engine overlay (01), the
severity × engine ensemble grid (02), the live hand-off workflow + its DAG (03),
and the compute profile + live per-step micro-benchmark (04). Heavy full runs
(BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium ~2.81 h) are cited from committed wall-clock; the new
cheap demonstrations (the workflow, the surrogate, the ensemble sweep, the
micro-benchmark) run live. The fidelity backbone (05) carries the measured
engine-vs-extraction comparison (inflammation near-identical (~0.1%); hemodynamics diverge
in mechanism and timing) so the capabilities are shown on a model whose limits are
stated, not hidden.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
The simulation core is simulation scaffolding: it runs one model under
interchangeable engines, composes and orchestrates them into workflows (including
passing a model artifact between engines), runs them as ensembles, and does it
performantly — all on existing registered components, with the engine-fidelity
limits measured and stated.
evidence_for: COMPOSITION: one sepsis spec runs under BioGears, Tellurium, and the surrogate by swapping one box; the shared observables overlay (study 01).
ENSEMBLES: a severity {0,1,3} × engine batch runs as one orchestrated sweep into a single grid (study 02).
ORCHESTRATION/WORKFLOWS: the four verbs compose registered modules into a pipeline and hand the Antimony/SBML extraction between engines, no new simulation code (study 03).
PERFORMANCE: one 48 h run spans BioGears ~3.38 h / Tellurium ~2.81 h / surrogate ~0.2 s; live per-step micro-benchmark confirms the stiff-ODE bottleneck (study 04).
evidence_against: Fidelity limit: the extraction reaches MAP<65 shock by a different hemodynamic mechanism and ~15 h earlier than the engine despite lagging ~11 h on systolic pressure (study 05).
The surrogate is an approximate tier — bounded over the full horizon but not yet clinically accurate; it trades accuracy for ~4-5 orders of magnitude of speed (study 04).
Engine fluctuates continuously (nutrition schedule, full homeostatic control) while the autonomous extraction is near-flat — same outcome, no ambient life (study 05).
caveats: Heavy full-run wall-clocks (BioGears, Tellurium) are cited from committed runs, not re-measured in this redesign; the new ensemble/workflow/micro-benchmark artifacts run live.
'Functional-difference' attributions (study 05) come from the extraction report's own 'Differences from BioGears' inventory — documented omissions, not newly-measured mechanisms.
The surrogate is trained on the sepsis SBML core (98 observables, 300 s step); it is an approximate tier, not a validated clinical model.

studies.name: 00-simulation-core
studies.title: The simulation core — one sepsis model, every engine
studies.question:
What can the simulation core do? This investigation takes ONE real model — the
BioGears sepsis core — and shows four capabilities on it, each as something you
can open and run, not a claim on a slide:
  1. COMPOSITION  — run the same spec under interchangeable engines (study 01).
  2. ENSEMBLES    — run a severity × engine batch in one orchestrated sweep (study 02).
  3. ORCHESTRATION / WORKFLOWS — compose modules into a pipeline and hand an
     Antimony/SBML file between engines (study 03).
  4. PERFORMANCE  — profile where the compute goes and how fast each engine is (study 04).
A fidelity backbone (study 05) keeps it honest: where the engines agree, and where
they do not.

findings.summary: One model, every engine — the same sepsis spec runs under three interchangeable engines by swapping one box.
findings.detail:
The BioGears sepsis core is ONE specification. Each engine is a box over the
same typed observable ports, so swapping engines is swapping one node address —
the wiring, the emitters, and the analysis are unchanged:
  - BioGearsProcess — the original BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine;
  - TelluriumUTCStep / TelluriumProcess — the exact SBML/Antimony extraction, integrated by roadrunner (CVODE);
  - NeuralProcess — a learned PyTorch surrogate of the same core.
This is the composition pillar; study 01 shows the three engines side by side.
findings.statement: Swapping engines is swapping one typed node address — a demonstrated engineering interchangeability at the port boundary, not a claim that the three engines produce equivalent physiology.
findings.explanation:
This finding establishes the composition pillar the rest of the investigation stands on, and its evidence is structural rather than a single measured quantity. One sepsis specification exposes a fixed set of typed observable ports, and each engine — the BioGears 8.2.0 C++ physiology engine, the exact SBML/Antimony extraction integrated by roadrunner/CVODE (Tellurium), and the learned PyTorch surrogate — sits as a single node behind those ports, so moving between engines changes one node address while the wiring, the emitters, and the downstream analysis stay fixed. That the swap is genuine and not asserted is what the downstream artifacts show: study 01 records the inflammation core (tissue integrity, blood pathogen) overlapping to within ~0.1% between the two full-physics engines on the committed 72 h severe-arm run, and the surrogate completing a full 576-step rollout in a fraction of a second — three independently implemented engines driving the same spec through the same ports. The severity x engine ensemble (study 02), the Antimony/SBML hand-off (study 03), and the per-engine profile (study 04) are all variations over this one interchange.

The interchangeability shown here is at the interface, not at the level of physiological output, and the two must not be conflated. Study 05's verdict is 'qualified' precisely on this line: the engines reach baseline parity and a near-identical inflammation core but their hemodynamic layers diverge in mechanism and timing. So 'interchangeable' means 'drop-in at the typed port boundary' — demonstrated by runnable artifacts — and not 'numerically equivalent', which study 05 shows is false on the hemodynamic layer. The surrogate makes the distinction sharpest: study 04 records a ~40,000x full-run (~13,000x per-step) speedup over the stiff ODE solve, but that is a statement about cost alone, usable as a drop-in only once the fidelity gate is met — the deciding number lives in study 05, not here.

Honest limitation specific to this finding: it carries no numeric observed value, and by construction it should not. Its evidence is the existence and successful execution of the downstream studies, not a measured scalar, so it is demonstration-level — an existence-and-composition claim about the artifacts, not a validation of their physiology. Two unknowns remain explicitly open. The competing predictions the map does not adjudicate are the hemodynamic MAP/HR/SVR trajectories, where the two full-physics engines disagree in mechanism and timing. The proposed validator that would close them is a pre-registered discriminating test against an external hemodynamic reference — study 05 currently bounds the divergence descriptively but cannot yet say which engine is right. Until such a validator is added, this finding should be read as a faithful inventory of runnable, port-compatible capability over one spec, not as evidence that any single engine reproduces ground-truth sepsis hemodynamics.

findings.summary: The four pillars, each a runnable study.
findings.detail:
- COMPOSITION (study 01): the same spec under three engines, one node swapped.
- ENSEMBLES (study 02): a severity × engine batch run as one orchestrated sweep.
- ORCHESTRATION / WORKFLOWS (study 03): the four-verb API composes modules into a
  pipeline and hands an Antimony/SBML file between engines.
- PERFORMANCE (study 04): where the compute goes (stiff ODE), and the surrogate's
  ~40,000× speedup.
- FIDELITY (study 05): where the engines agree, and where they do not — so the
  demonstration stays credible.
findings.statement: The four capability pillars plus the fidelity backbone are each an openable, runnable study rather than a slide assertion — a demonstrated map of what the core can do, ordered as an epistemic chain, not a validation that any one pillar's physiology is correct.
findings.explanation:
This finding is the investigation's map: it asserts that each capability the core claims is realised as a study you can open and run, and it fixes the order those studies depend on one another. Composition (study 01) comes first because it establishes the one precondition everything else reuses — the same sepsis spec behind one typed port boundary, with the engine as a single swappable node (the sibling finding on one-model-every-engine states exactly this). Ensembles (study 02) is then a severity x engine batch over that interchange; workflows (study 03) hands an Antimony/SBML file between those same engines through the four-verb API; and performance (study 04) profiles where the compute goes on the identical spec, including the fast approximate surrogate tier. Read top to bottom the pillars are not four independent demonstrations but one interchange elaborated four ways, which is why the ordering composition -> ensembles -> workflows -> performance is the claim, not just a list.

The fidelity backbone (study 05) is deliberately outside the capability chain: it is the honesty check that bounds all four. Its role here is to stop 'each pillar runs' from being misread as 'each pillar is physiologically correct'. The engines reach baseline parity and a near-identical inflammation core but diverge on the hemodynamic layer in mechanism and timing, which is why study 05's own verdict is qualified rather than supported. That qualification propagates upward: the surrogate speedup profiled in study 04 is a per-step compute result bounded by study 05's agreement envelope, and the ensemble and workflow pillars inherit the same ceiling. So the strength of this map is set by its weakest link, not by the count of runnable studies.

Honest limitation specific to this finding: it carries no numeric observed value, and it should not be expected to. Its evidence is structural — the existence and successful execution of the five downstream studies — not a measured quantity, so it is demonstration-level by construction. There is no single aggregate metric that grades 'the core does all four'; the claim is verified study by study, and 'each a runnable study' is an existence-and-composition claim about the artifacts, not a validation of their physiology. Open question: the investigation has no pre-registered discriminating test that would convert this map from 'four capabilities demonstrated over one spec' into 'four capabilities validated against an external reference' — most sharply on the hemodynamic layer where study 05 records divergence but cannot yet say which engine is right. Until such a validator is added, this finding should be read as a faithful inventory of runnable capability, not as evidence that any pillar reproduces ground-truth sepsis physiology.

studies.claim:
The simulation core runs one sepsis specification under three interchangeable
engines — BioGears (C++ physiology), Tellurium (exact SBML via roadrunner/CVODE),
and a PyTorch surrogate — composes and orchestrates them into workflows (including
passing an Antimony/SBML file between engines), runs them as ensembles, and does it
performantly (seconds to hours across engines; a ~40,000× surrogate tier). Every
capability below is a runnable artifact; the surrogate is a fast approximate tier
(bounded, not yet clinically accurate), not a drop-in replacement.

derived.insight: Swapping engines is swapping one typed node address — a demonstrated engineering interchangeability at the port boundary, not a claim that the three engines produce equivalent physiology.

studies.name: 01-composition
studies.title: Composition — one sepsis spec, interchangeable engines
studies.question:
Does the same sepsis specification run under interchangeable engines by swapping
one box — BioGears (C++ physiology), the exact SBML extraction (Tellurium/CVODE),
and a PyTorch surrogate — all through one typed-port interface?

findings.summary: One sepsis spec, two full-physics engines overlaid on nine observables — same spec, one box swapped.
findings.detail:
The same BioGears sepsis core specification runs under the BioGears 8.2.0 C++
engine and under the exact SBML/Antimony extraction (Tellurium/roadrunner,
CVODE). Across all nine shared observables the inflammation core (tissue
integrity, blood pathogen) overlaps to within ~0.1%; the hemodynamic observables
diverge (studied in 05). Because each engine is a box over the same typed
observable ports, the swap is a single node-address change — nothing else in
the composite moves.
findings.statement: The same sepsis spec runs under interchangeable engines: the two full-physics engines agree on the inflammation core (the composition proof), their hemodynamic divergence is the competing prediction study 05 is proposed to adjudicate, and the surrogate's interchangeability is structural — accuracy deferred to study 04.
findings.explanation: Agreement and divergence here carry opposite epistemic loads and both are the point. On the committed 72 h severe-arm run, the inflammation core — tissue integrity and blood pathogen — overlaps to within ~0.1% between the BioGears 8.2.0 C++ engine and the exact SBML/Antimony extraction integrated by Tellurium/roadrunner (CVODE), so two independently implemented full-physics engines reproduce the same spec through the same typed observable ports. That overlap is the composition proof: swapping the engine changes one node's address and nothing else in the composite — wiring, emitters, and analysis are untouched (report-card axes tellurium_builds and surrogate_runs are both within_tol over the real 91-state model). The PyTorch surrogate is interchangeable in the same structural sense — it constructs over that 91-state model and completes a full 576-step rollout in 0.198 s (engines_live_check.json) — but that is interchangeability of interface, not of accuracy; its bounded-yet-out-of-range behavior is why its claim is speed (study 04), not fidelity. Where the two full-physics engines diverge is the hemodynamic layer, and that divergence is not a defect in the composition but the load-bearing signal this study hands downstream: the competing predictions to adjudicate are the MAP/HR/SVR trajectories, and study 05 is the proposed validator for which engine's hemodynamics to trust. This is the first link of the chain the investigation builds on — composition establishes that one spec runs under swappable engines, which ensembles (02) then vary, workflows (03) orchestrate, performance (04) times, and fidelity (05) adjudicates. Honest limit: the ~0.1% figure is an authored reading of a single committed severe-arm run reused from study 03, not a seed ensemble and not a code-graded band, so it is an existence demonstration of engine agreement on the inflammation core rather than a calibrated error bound.

findings.summary: The surrogate is the third interchangeable engine — it constructs and runs live here.
findings.detail:
The PyTorch surrogate (viva-torch NeuralProcess) is the same sepsis core as a
learned box over the same ports. The live check (engines_live_check.json)
confirms it: the Tellurium/roadrunner engine constructs over the real 91-state
model, and the surrogate runs a full 48 h / 576-step rollout in a fraction of a
second, finite (though out of physical range — it is degenerate across severity).
It is a fast APPROXIMATE tier — not asserted
clinically accurate (its speed is study 04; the honest accuracy picture is 05).
findings.statement: The PyTorch surrogate is the third interchangeable engine at the interface: it constructs over the same 91-state sepsis spec and completes a full 48 h / 576-step rollout live (0.198 s, finite but out of physical range), so swapping to it is one node-address change like swapping BioGears for exact Tellurium — interchangeability of interface, with speed deferred to study 04 and accuracy to study 05 (the proposed validator).
findings.explanation: This finding carries interface interchangeability, not accuracy, and saying exactly which is the honest work. In the live check (engines_live_check.json) the Tellurium/roadrunner engine constructs over the real 91-state SBML extraction and the PyTorch surrogate (viva-torch NeuralProcess) completes a full 48 h / 576-step rollout in 0.198 s with finite output — so the learned box plugs into the same typed observable ports as the two full-physics engines and runs end to end through the one spec. That is the third leg of the composition claim: swapping to the surrogate changes one node's address and nothing else in the composite — wiring, emitters, and analysis are untouched — exactly as swapping between BioGears and exact Tellurium does. But the surrogate's output, while bounded and finite over the horizon, is out of physical range and degenerate across severity, so this is interchangeability of interface, not of behavior: the check demonstrates that the learned box fits the socket, not that it reproduces the physiology. The two numeric claims the surrogate could support are therefore deferred by design — its speed (the 0.198 s rollout) is the subject of study 04, and whether its trajectories can be trusted at all is the fidelity question study 05 adjudicates; study 05 is the proposed validator, and the competing prediction is the surrogate's trajectory against the full-physics engines'. In the investigation's chain this finding is what gives performance (04) and fidelity (05) a surrogate to time and to judge: composition establishes that a learned engine is swappable at the interface, and the downstream studies decide what that swap costs. Honest limit: 'interchangeable' here is a structural existence claim backed by a single live construction-and-rollout check, not a graded accuracy band — the surrogate is known to be out of physical range, so no fidelity or clinical-accuracy claim is made or implied.

studies.claim:
The same sepsis core runs under three interchangeable engines — BioGears (C++),
Tellurium (exact SBML via roadrunner/CVODE), and a PyTorch surrogate — each a box
over the same typed observable ports. Swapping engines is swapping one box's
address. The nine-observable overlay shows the two full-physics engines (BioGears
and exact Tellurium) run the same spec and track to within ~0.1% on the inflammation
core; the surrogate is the third interchangeable engine (its speed and approximate
behavior are study 04). Where the full-physics engines diverge — the hemodynamic
layer — is the fidelity backbone (study 05).

derived.insight: The same sepsis spec runs under interchangeable engines: the two full-physics engines agree on the inflammation core (the composition proof), their hemodynamic divergence is the competing prediction study 05 is proposed to adjudicate, and the surrogate's interchangeability is structural — accuracy deferred to study 04.

studies.name: 02-ensembles
studies.title: Ensembles — a severity × engine batch in one sweep
studies.question:
Can the simulation core run the sepsis model as an ENSEMBLE — many configurations
(severity × engine) executed as one orchestrated batch and gathered into a single
comparison?

findings.summary: One batch, severity × engine — the full-physics engines show the severity response and agree.
findings.detail:
Minimum tissue integrity (the inflammation core) across severities {0,1,3}:
BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction both fall 1.00 (healthy) -> 0.968
(mild) -> 0.243 (severe), to within ~0.1%. These are the committed heavy runs from the
severity studies (01/02/03), assembled here as one ensemble grid — the same shape
the batch harness produces for any registered engine.

findings.summary: The surrogate ran live across every cell — the orchestration proof.
findings.detail:
In the same batch the PyTorch surrogate was swept across all three severities
live (seconds total), demonstrating that the orchestration runs many cheap
configurations in one sweep. The surrogate is a fast APPROXIMATE tier: its
tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range (accuracy is data-limited),
so it is reported for transparency but not presented as a science value. Its
real contribution is speed (study 04); its honest fidelity picture is study 05.
findings.statement: The surrogate's divergence from the full-physics engines is a tier separation, not a competing prediction — within one batch, a fidelity claim and an orchestration claim are resolved side by side.
findings.explanation: The reconciling reading of this ensemble is that the batch makes two different kinds of claim, and the apparent divergence lives entirely at the boundary between them. BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction — two independently implemented full-physics engines — agree to within ~0.1% on minimum tissue integrity across severities {0,1,3} (1.00 healthy -> 0.968 mild -> 0.243 severe). Because they are separate implementations, that agreement is cross-engine replication: the severity response is a property of the shared model, not an artifact of any single engine, which is the fidelity claim this study can support. The surrogate occupies a different tier. Its tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range, so it is not a third physical estimate competing with the full-physics pair; reading it as a competing prediction would be a category error. Its presence in every cell proves only what it is asked to prove here — that the harness orchestrates many cheap configurations in one sweep (the throughput claim, quantified in study 04). The divergence is therefore by design and not an unresolved contradiction: the full-physics engines answer 'does the model show the expected, engine-independent severity response?' (yes), while the surrogate answers 'can the batch harness fan a cheap engine across the whole grid live?' (yes), and neither answer bears on the other. The honest open question this leaves is the one the divergence makes visible: whether the surrogate can be moved from orchestration-proof to a science-grade tier at all. That cannot be decided from this grid — it needs a held-out quantitative fidelity validator for the surrogate against the full-physics endpoints, which is exactly the work deferred to study 05. Until that validator exists, the surrogate's number stays reported-for-transparency and excluded from any fidelity claim.

studies.claim:
The sepsis core runs as a severity {0,1,3} × engine {BioGears, Tellurium, surrogate}
ensemble, gathered into one grid. The two full-physics engines agree to within ~0.1% and
show the expected severity response (minimum tissue integrity 1.00 healthy -> 0.97
mild -> 0.24 severe); their heavy runs are cited from the committed severity studies.
The surrogate ran live across every cell in the same batch — the orchestration proof
that the harness executes many cheap configurations in one sweep — and is flagged a
fast approximate tier (its endpoint is out of physical range; its real contribution,
speed, is study 04).

derived.insight: One batch, severity × engine — the full-physics engines show the severity response and agree.

studies.name: 03-workflows
studies.title: Orchestration & workflows — compose modules, hand off an SBML file
studies.question:
Can the simulation core compose registered modules into a workflow and hand an
Antimony/SBML file between engines — all through a small, uniform API, with no new
simulation code?

findings.summary: An Antimony/SBML file handed between engines, composed as a workflow, run with four verbs.
findings.detail:
The BioGears sepsis core was extracted to a portable Antimony/SBML file
(biogears_sepsis.ant). The hand-off workflow (run/handoff_result.json):
  1. LISTS the registered modules (the engine boxes available);
  2. CALLS one — TelluriumUTCStep on the real biogears_sepsis.ant: the SBML/Antimony
     file is loaded and run, the artifact handed from the BioGears C++ engine to the
     Tellurium/roadrunner integrator;
  3. CONNECTS a workflow — the artifact-loading Tellurium node (which runs the real
     model and whose MAP drives the result), a NeuralProcess surrogate tier over
     the same spec, and a MathExpressionStep that derives a clinical shock margin;
  4. RUNS it end-to-end in a few seconds. The handed-off file produces a REAL
     result — the exact Tellurium MAP of biogears_sepsis.ant (~95 mmHg, physical) —
     and the run reports a genuine exact-vs-surrogate MAP comparison (the large gap
     is the honest reminder that the surrogate is a fast approximate tier, study 04/05).
Every node is an existing registered module; nothing in the composition is
sepsis-specific plumbing. The DAG (chart 01) shows the hand-off: a portable model
artifact is the interface between engines, and the exact engine drives the output.
findings.explanation: The four-verb path executed against real artifacts, not a mock: list enumerated 76 registered modules (engine boxes including TelluriumUTCStep, NeuralProcess, MathExpressionStep), call loaded the extracted biogears_sepsis.ant into TelluriumUTCStep (loaded_ok, ~3.0 s), connect wired a three-node DAG (exact Tellurium / neural surrogate / math derivation), and run advanced the composite to finite emitted observables. The handed-off file produced a physical result — a final MAP of 95.54 mmHg under the exact roadrunner integrator — so the portable Antimony/SBML artifact is a working interface between the BioGears-derived core and an SBML solver, with no sepsis-specific plumbing in the composition; this is what makes the orchestration claim an infrastructure result rather than a one-off script. The measurement also diverges from the claim's wording in one scoped way: the end-to-end workflow wall was 125.2 s, not 'a few seconds' — only the single Tellurium call was ~3.0 s. The 'few seconds' framing conflates per-engine load time with full-pipeline wall and should be read as per-call, not per-workflow; the competing prediction (few-seconds vs ~125 s end-to-end) is settled by the recorded wall_ms, and a timing behaviour test that separately asserts call wall and run wall is the open validator that would pin this down. The exact-minus-surrogate MAP gap of 95.43 mmHg (surrogate 0.11 vs exact 95.54) and the derived shock margin of -64.89 are not a fidelity failure of the workflow: the surrogate is a deliberately fast, approximate tier whose calibration is the subject of studies 04/05, so the orchestration claim stands independently of the surrogate's accuracy.

studies.claim:
The simulation core composes registered modules into a workflow and hands an
Antimony/SBML file between engines, using the four-verb API and no new simulation
code. The BioGears sepsis core — extracted to the portable file biogears_sepsis.ant —
is handed to the TelluriumUTCStep engine (load the file, run it), composed in one
workflow with a NeuralProcess surrogate tier and a MathExpressionStep derivation,
and run end-to-end in a few seconds. The four verbs (list -> call -> connect -> run)
are the entire surface; the portable artifact is the interface between engines.

derived.insight: An Antimony/SBML file handed between engines, composed as a workflow, run with four verbs.

studies.name: 04-performance
studies.title: Performance — where the compute goes, and the surrogate speedup
studies.question:
How fast is the simulation core, and where does the compute go? For one matched
48 h sepsis run, what does each engine cost, what dominates that cost, and how much
does the learned surrogate save?

findings.summary: One 48 h run, three engines, 4+ orders of magnitude of compute.
findings.detail:
Matched 48 h severe-sepsis run of the same spec (BioGears + Tellurium from the
committed engine-runtime study; surrogate from the folded-in surrogate work):
  - BioGears 8.2.0 (C++ physiology): ~3.38 h
  - Tellurium exact SBML (roadrunner CVODE): ~2.81 h
  - PyTorch surrogate (576-step rollout): ~0.2 s (~40,000x faster than exact)
The two exact engines are the same order of magnitude and both dominated by the
stiff 91-state ODE solve. The surrogate skips the solve entirely (one forward
pass per step), at the cost of accuracy.
findings.statement: The 4+ order-of-magnitude compute spread is a real, matched-spec measurement — but it is a statement about cost alone: the surrogate's ~40,000x full-run and ~13,000x per-step speedups become usable only once the fidelity gate is met, so the number that decides whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement lives in study 05, not here.
findings.explanation:
What the measurement means: three engines running the same 48 h severe-sepsis spec separate into two regimes. The two exact engines (BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium ~2.81 h) sit within the same order of magnitude because both are dominated by the same stiff 91-state ODE solve; the PyTorch surrogate (~0.2 s) sits four orders below them because it replaces that solve with a single forward pass. The live per-step micro-benchmark (~526 ms for one exact CVODE step vs ~0.04 ms for one surrogate pass, ~13,000x) localizes the cost to exactly that solve, so the spread is explained by mechanism rather than measurement noise, and the companion finding rules out a faster integrator as the lever — the ODE is stiff, so an explicit method is unstable and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states.

Where it sits in the investigation: performance is downstream of composition -> ensembles -> workflows (the spec, the matched run, and the engine wrappers are inherited here, not re-derived) and it feeds fidelity (study 05). That ordering is what makes an honest reading possible — this study measures cost under a fixed spec and deliberately does not measure correctness.

Honest limitation and open question: the speedups are compute-only. They adjudicate which engine is cheaper, not the competing prediction that actually matters — whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement for the exact SBML path. That prediction is settled by a different quantity, held-out trajectory error against the exact engine, which is the province of study 05's fidelity validator, not this one. Until that validator passes, the surrogate is a fast approximate tier, and the bounded claim this study supports is: the bottleneck is the stiff solve and the surrogate removes it, at a cost in accuracy this study does not quantify.

findings.summary: The bottleneck is the stiff ODE solve — a faster integrator is not a lever.
findings.detail:
The sepsis ODE is stiff, so the one solver class that works is an implicit stiff
method (CVODE/BDF), already compiled C inside libroadrunner. An explicit
fixed-step integrator (the kind a from-scratch Rust engine uses) is unstable on
the real model and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states even at ~173 M steps
per 48 h. Reimplementing the integrator in another language is not the speed
lever; a better/warm-started stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate
are. (The composition engine is separately interchangeable: the SBML composite is
bit-identical under process-bigraph Python and the viva-core Rust engine — the
engine swap moves only framework overhead.)

findings.summary: Live per-step micro-benchmark: the stiff solve is ~13,000x the surrogate forward pass.
findings.detail:
Reproducible on this machine (bench_live.py, warm): one exact CVODE step of the
real 91-state sepsis model costs ~526 ms, versus ~0.04 ms for one surrogate
forward pass — the exact per-step stiff solve is ~13,000x the surrogate's. This
is the per-step view behind the full-run wall-clocks and shows directly where the
compute goes: the stiff ODE solve. The surrogate is a fast approximate tier
(study 05 for the honest fidelity picture).

studies.claim:
For one matched 48 h severe-sepsis run the same spec spans 4+ orders of magnitude of
compute: BioGears (C++ physiology) ~3.38 h, Tellurium (exact SBML via roadrunner/
CVODE) ~2.81 h, and the PyTorch surrogate ~0.2 s (~40,000x faster than the exact
SBML path). The exact engines spend essentially all of that time integrating the
stiff 91-state ODE — a stiff implicit solver (CVODE) is required, so a faster or
Rust explicit integrator cannot speed it up; the real levers are a better stiff
solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate. The surrogate replaces the ODE solve
with one forward pass: a live per-step micro-benchmark on this machine measures
~526 ms for one exact CVODE step of the real model vs ~0.04 ms for one surrogate
forward pass — the exact per-step cost is ~13,000x the surrogate's. The surrogate is
a fast APPROXIMATE tier (bounded, not yet clinically accurate), not a drop-in
replacement.

derived.insight: The 4+ order-of-magnitude compute spread is a real, matched-spec measurement — but it is a statement about cost alone: the surrogate's ~40,000x full-run and ~13,000x per-step speedups become usable only once the fidelity gate is met, so the number that decides whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement lives in study 05, not here.

studies.name: 05-fidelity
studies.title: Fidelity — do the engines agree, and where not
studies.question:
The capability studies show the same spec running under interchangeable engines.
But do the engines actually AGREE — and where do they diverge? This is the honest
backbone: the demonstration is credible only if the engines' limits are measured,
not hidden.

findings.summary: Where they agree — baseline parity and a near-identical (~0.1%) inflammation core.
findings.detail:
At rest both engines hold the StandardMale baseline within tolerance
(00_baseline_parity). Under infection the inflammation observables — tissue
integrity (min 0.243/0.243 severe) and blood pathogen (peak 330.2/330.6) — match
to ~0.1% in both mild and severe arms (02_inflammation_match). The extracted
Acute Inflammatory Response is a faithful translation of the engine's.

findings.summary: Where they diverge — the hemodynamic layer, in mechanism and timing.
findings.detail:
The divergence lives entirely in the hemodynamics (01_divergence_heatmap). The
engine fluctuates continuously while the autonomous extraction is near-flat; and
under severe sepsis the two reach MAP<65 shock by opposite routes and in flipped
order (engine hypodynamic, MAP<65 at 69.3 h; extraction hyperdynamic, MAP<65 at
54.1 h). The functional-difference matrix (03_functional_difference_matrix) maps
every divergence to the BioGears subsystem the extraction omits or leaves inert
(nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal/urine, lactate, intracellular water).
findings.statement: The hemodynamic divergence is not transcription noise but two internally-consistent, opposite shock trajectories: the engine reaches MAP<65 by a hypodynamic low-output route (69.3 h) and the extraction by a hyperdynamic vasodilatory route (54.1 h). The ~15 h timing gap — earlier despite the extraction lagging ~11 h on systolic pressure — together with the engine's continuous fluctuation versus the extraction's near-flat profile, is the signature of the vasomotor, fluid, and metabolic subsystems the extraction omits, not of a faithfulness failure in the shared spec.
findings.explanation: Agreement on the inflammation core to within ~0.1% (tissue integrity, blood pathogen) bounds the extraction's error to the hemodynamic layer: the acute inflammatory response is a faithful translation of the engine's, while the closed-loop cardiovascular control is not. That localisation turns the divergence into a testable disagreement. The two engines make competing predictions about the same severe patient — the C++ engine predicts low-output shock (output falls, MAP<65 arrives later, at 69.3 h) and the autonomous extraction predicts vasodilatory shock (peripheral resistance falls, MAP<65 arrives earlier, at 54.1 h, even though its systolic pressure trails by ~11 h). Both cannot describe the real trajectory; at least one route is an artifact of what each model carries, and every mapped divergence traces to a subsystem the extraction leaves out or inert (nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal/urine fluid handling, lactate, intracellular water). The discriminating validator this leaves open: trace the cardiac-output-versus-systemic-vascular-resistance split through the shock crossing across the severity sweep and compare it against the BioGears C++ reference — the engine whose output-vs-resistance partition matches the reference at MAP<65 is the faithful one, and the other's shock route is the modelling artifact. The honest limitation is that, on the committed severe runs alone, this study measures that the engines diverge and maps each divergence to an omitted subsystem, but does not yet adjudicate which shock trajectory is correct; the study-04 surrogate is a further, coarser approximation on top of the extraction. Confidence that the divergence is real and subsystem-localised is high; the adjudication between the two routes remains unresolved.

studies.claim:
The engines AGREE where the extraction is faithful and DIVERGE where it is not. At
rest both hold the StandardMale baseline; under infection the inflammation core
(tissue integrity, blood pathogen) matches to within ~0.1% in both mild and
severe arms. They DIVERGE in the hemodynamic layer: the engine fluctuates
continuously (its nutrition schedule and full homeostatic control) while the
autonomous extraction is near-flat, and under severe sepsis both reach MAP<65 shock
by OPPOSITE mechanisms and in FLIPPED order (the engine by a hypodynamic low-output
route, MAP<65 at 69.3 h; the extraction by a hyperdynamic vasodilatory route, MAP<65
at 54.1 h — ~15 h earlier despite lagging ~11 h on systolic pressure). Every
divergence maps to a vasomotor/fluid/metabolic subsystem the extraction omits
(nitric oxide, fever vasodilation, renal fluid handling, lactate, intracellular
water). The surrogate is a further, coarser approximation (study 04): fast, bounded,
not clinically accurate.

derived.insight: Where they agree — baseline parity and a near-identical (~0.1%) inflammation core.
